input:
When it comes to characterising a gas emission, the question of how the sample is taken is just as important as the analysis that is subsequently performed on it, because a poorly taken sample can undermine even the most careful laboratory work. Representative sampling is concerned with ensuring that the material actually collected faithfully reflects the emission as a whole, across both the duct cross-section and the period over which the emission is being characterised.

Firstly, the location at which samples are taken matters a great deal. The sampling point needs to be positioned where the gas stream is as well mixed as possible, so that the concentration measured at that point is genuinely indicative of the stream as a whole rather than of a local pocket or a stratified layer. In practice, this means thinking carefully about the effects of bends, junctions and other disturbances, and about whether a single point can adequately represent a stream whose composition may vary across its width.

Secondly, a single sample is rarely built from a single act of collection. Instead, several increments are typically collected over the sampling period and combined to form one sample for analysis, so that short-term fluctuations in the emission are averaged out rather than captured by chance. Last but not least, it is worth emphasising why a single grab sample can be so misleading: an emission is not constant over time, and a grab sample freezes one moment, which may coincide with a peak, a lull, or a transient that bears little relation to the emission's typical behaviour.
target:
Representative sampling of a gas emission has one requirement: the material collected must stand for the emission as a whole, over the full cross-section of the duct and over the whole period the sample claims to cover. Every choice in the sampling procedure is judged against that requirement.

The sampling point is placed where the gas is well mixed. A stream leaving a bend or a junction can be stratified, with concentration varying across the duct, and a probe in such a stream measures the layer it sits in rather than the stream. A point measurement represents the emission only where the composition at the point matches the average composition across the section, so the location is chosen away from disturbances, and a traverse across the section is used where mixing cannot be assumed. The sampling rate and the probe arrangement are held steady during collection, because a varying draw distorts the share of the stream that reaches the sample.

One sample is built from several increments collected across the sampling period and combined before analysis. Each increment is a small portion of the gas taken at its moment; combined, the increments average the fluctuations of the emission over the period instead of reporting whichever moment a single collection happened to catch. The number of increments and their spacing follow the variability of the source: a steady emission needs fewer increments than one that swings with the process cycle.

A single grab sample misleads for exactly this reason. An emission varies over time as the process load changes, and a grab sample freezes one instant of that variation. The result is a true measurement of the instant and a false picture of the period: a peak reads as the typical level, a lull reads as compliance, and neither can be corrected afterwards, because the sample carries no record of the variation it missed.
